# Learn the meaning before the syntax

A language is not its keywords. The questions that matter are **who owns a value, what the type checker promises, how concurrent work is coordinated, and when code actually runs**. Each language here is taught through those questions, from a ten-year-old's picture of the idea to the runtime structure that implements it.

## The languages

| Language | Chapters | The ideas that explain most of it |
|---|---|---|
| [Go](go/index.qmd) | 15 | Values and slices, implicit interfaces, errors as values, and above all [goroutines](go/09-goroutines-and-the-scheduler.qmd), [channels](go/10-channels.qmd), [select and context](go/11-select-and-context.qmd) and the [memory model](go/12-sync-and-the-memory-model.qmd) |
| [Python](python/index.qmd) | 13 | [Names bound to objects](python/01-names-objects-and-references.qmd), generators and decorators, the data model and MRO, the [GIL](python/12-threads-processes-and-the-gil.qmd) and [asyncio](python/13-coroutines-and-asyncio.qmd) |
| [JavaScript](javascript/index.qmd) | 12 | [Coercion](javascript/01-values-types-and-coercion.qmd), closures, `this`, prototypes, and the [event loop](javascript/07-the-event-loop.qmd) behind promises and async/await |
| [TypeScript](typescript/index.qmd) | 12 | [Types as sets of shapes](typescript/01-structural-typing.qmd), narrowing, generics, mapped and conditional types, and where the type system is [deliberately unsound](typescript/12-variance-and-soundness.qmd) |
| [C#](csharp/index.qmd) | 13 | [Value versus reference types](csharp/01-value-and-reference-types.qmd), nullable types, reified generics, LINQ, pattern matching, and [async/await](csharp/11-tasks-and-async-await.qmd) |
| [Prolog](prolog/index.qmd) | 10 | Programs as logic, [unification](prolog/02-unification.qmd), [backtracking search](prolog/03-resolution-and-backtracking.qmd), constraints and grammars |
| [Rust](rust/index.qmd) | 16 | [Ownership](rust/01-ownership.qmd), borrowing and lifetimes, traits, and thread safety checked at compile time |
| [Java](java.qmd) | JVM path | Object references and generics, then the [JVM and the Java Memory Model](java/jvm/index.qmd) |

## How every chapter is built

The Go, Python, JavaScript, TypeScript, C# and Prolog chapters share one layout, so you always know where to look:

1. **The problem:** a concrete situation with real values, and what goes wrong without the concept.
2. **Explain it like I'm ten:** an everyday analogy, with the words of the language's designers and well-known teachers.
3. **From simple to advanced:** levels that each add one idea, with its math and a short piece of code.
4. **How it works underneath:** the runtime or compiler mechanism, taken from the official source.
5. **Common mistakes:** each with its exact error message and the fix.
6. **Interview questions:** with precise answers.
7. **Summary** and **References.**

**The code you read is the code that runs.** Every code block is cut from a lab next to the chapter that checks each quoted result and prints `OK`. Go labs run under the race detector, TypeScript labs prove their type errors with `@ts-expect-error`, and C# labs must build without a single warning. Code that cannot run, such as a compile error, is marked `sketch` and shown with the compiler's real message.

**Math states the core idea in one line.** After every formula comes a list of what each symbol means and an example with the chapter's own numbers. For instance, Go's rule for when a channel send must wait, $\operatorname{len}(c) = \operatorname{cap}(c) \land R(c) = 0$, is worked through with a channel of capacity 2.

## One question, many answers

The same operation means different things in different languages. That difference, not the syntax, is what to learn first.

**Passing a value to a function.** Does the callee get its own copy, a borrow, or another name for the same object?

| Language | What the callee receives |
|---|---|
| Go | A copy of the argument, though a copied slice header or pointer still reaches the same memory ([values and pointers](go/01-values-types-and-pointers.qmd), [slices](go/02-slices-and-maps.qmd)) |
| Python, JavaScript | Another name for the same object; mutating it is visible to the caller ([Python](python/01-names-objects-and-references.qmd), [JavaScript](javascript/01-values-types-and-coercion.qmd)) |
| C# | A copy for a `struct`, a copied reference for a `class`, or the variable itself with `ref` ([value and reference types](csharp/01-value-and-reference-types.qmd)) |
| Rust | The value moved, or a borrow the compiler tracks ([ownership](rust/01-ownership.qmd), [borrowing](rust/02-borrowing.qmd)) |
| Java | A copy of a primitive, or a copy of an object reference ([Java](java.qmd)) |
| Prolog | No assignment at all: arguments are unified, and a variable is bound at most once ([unification](prolog/02-unification.qmd)) |

**Doing two things at once.** What runs concurrently, and what keeps it safe?

| Language | Unit of concurrency | What coordinates it |
|---|---|---|
| Go | Goroutines multiplexed onto OS threads | Channels, `select`, `context`, and `sync` ([scheduler](go/09-goroutines-and-the-scheduler.qmd), [channels](go/10-channels.qmd)) |
| Python | Threads under the GIL, processes, or coroutines on one event loop | Locks and queues, or `await` ([GIL](python/12-threads-processes-and-the-gil.qmd), [asyncio](python/13-coroutines-and-asyncio.qmd)) |
| JavaScript | One thread running tasks and microtasks to completion | The event loop and promises ([event loop](javascript/07-the-event-loop.qmd)) |
| C# | Tasks on the thread pool | `async`/`await`, locks, `Interlocked` and channels ([tasks](csharp/11-tasks-and-async-await.qmd), [threads](csharp/12-threads-and-synchronisation.qmd)) |
| Rust | OS threads and futures | `Send` and `Sync` checked by the compiler ([concurrency](rust/10-concurrency.qmd), [async](rust/11-async-await.qmd)) |
| Java | Threads, including virtual threads | `synchronized`, `volatile` and the Java Memory Model ([JMM](java/jvm/jmm/index.qmd)) |

**The right question is not which language is best. It is what each language guarantees at the exact operation you are trying to understand.**

## Run the labs

Each language page gives the command for one lab. From the repository root, one command checks every chapter against the standard and runs every lab:

```bash
node --test programming-languages/check-languages.test.mjs
ONLY=go/10-channels node --test programming-languages/check-languages.test.mjs   # just one chapter
```

It needs Go 1.27, Python 3.14, Node 26, .NET 10 and SWI-Prolog, plus `npm ci` in `programming-languages/typescript/labs` for the TypeScript compiler. The Rust chapters have their own [examples and checks](rust/examples/index.qmd).
